lesson.title: Capstone: De Brug Reading
lesson.subtitle: one connected Dutch story with every bridge, tense and connector in plain sight

hook.title: The Whole Trail in One Page
hook.content: This is the reading capstone. Every sentence uses material you have already built: the twins, the articles, the V2 order, the past, the perfect, the connectors. Read it slowly and let the pieces line up.

pattern.title: Read for structure, not for vocabulary
pattern.content: Ik woon in een klein huis bij het water. Elke ochtend maak ik koffie en eet ik brood. Ik werk in de stad en kom 's avonds thuis. Het leven is gezellig. The words are simple; the structure is the whole course.
pattern.linguist_note: This passage deliberately combines direct twins, de/het, V2, present tense, a time phrase and a compound; it is a diagnostic of the whole course.
pattern.trap_note: Do not stop at every unknown word. The sentence frame tells you what the word must be doing; that is the reading skill the trail has built.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Capstone: De Brug Reading):
exercises.target_answer: het water, het huis, het brood, de koffie, werken, gezellig
exercises.meaning: water, house, bread, coffee, to work, cosy, convivial
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Capstone: De Brug Reading": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “I live in a small house by the water.”?
options: Ik woon in een klein huis bij het water.
Ik woon in een kleine huis bij het water.
Ik woon bij het water in een klein huis.
exercises.target_answer: Ik woon in een klein huis bij het water.
exercises.meaning: I live in a small house by the water.
exercises.explanation: “Ik woon in een klein huis bij het water.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Capstone: De Brug Reading”.

exercises.idea: Every morning I make coffee and eat bread.
cues: The pattern: Read for structure, not for vocabulary
It means: Every morning I make coffee and eat bread.
idea_parts: Every morning I make coffee and eat bread.
exercises.target_answer: Elke ochtend maak ik koffie en eet ik brood.
exercises.meaning: Every morning I make coffee and eat bread.
exercises.explanation: “Elke ochtend maak ik koffie en eet ik brood.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Read for structure, not for vocabulary.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not stop at every unknown word. The sentence frame tells you what the word must be doing; that is the reading skill the trail has built.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.german: Ik werk in de stad en kom 's avonds thuis.
exercises.natural: I work in the city and come home in the evening.
options: I work in the city and come in the evening home.
I work in the city and come home in the evening.
You work in the city and come in the evening home.
exercises.target_answer: I work in the city and come in the evening home.
exercises.meaning: I work in the city and come home in the evening.
exercises.explanation: “Ik werk in de stad en kom 's avonds thuis.” is word-for-word “I work in the city and come in the evening home.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Read for structure, not for vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Het leven is gezellig.” reuses only material taught in “Capstone: De Brug Reading” — Read for structure, not for vocabulary.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het leven is gezellig.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Read for structure, not for vocabulary.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “Tomorrow I will work again.”
twist.explanation: Morgen is fronted, so the verb comes second: ga ik. Weer ('again') sits before the infinitive.

summary.outcome: Read a connected Dutch passage and recognise every structure from the trail.
summary.takeaway: The course ends where it began: ordinary Dutch sentences, read through patterns you already own.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: De Brug Review.

water.etymology_derivation: English water and Dutch water are direct twins; German shifted t to ss in Wasser.

huis.etymology_derivation: English house and Dutch huis are the same word; ui answers to ou.

brood.etymology_derivation: English bread and Dutch brood are the same word with different vowels.

koffie.etymology_derivation: The same loan chain as English coffee, through Dutch.

werken.etymology_derivation: English work and Dutch werken are the same verb.

gezellig.etymology_derivation: From gezel ('companion'); it describes shared warmth, not just a room.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
